RAPID SITUATION ASSESSMENT · NEPAL · META DATA THROUGH 31 AUG 04:45 NPT

Bhote Koshi Flood — Population & Connectivity Assessment

This report is an interpretation of population dynamics following the 26 August 2026 glacial-lake-outburst flood on the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. The principal basis of the analysis is a five-day time-series of Meta's Data for Good crisis signals (population, network connectivity, and movement) set against the Copernicus EMSR927 rapid mapping activation data and four ground-truth situation reports.

Key finding

Despite a momentary recovery of population signals in the Rasuwa disaster epicenter on the evening of August 27th, mobility data from Meta is now consistently measuring a roughly 50% reduction of population in this area. Network signals from the disaster epicenter continue to improve, making it unlikely that this finding is simply a data error. It is not possible based on this data, however, to determine exactly which signals are from a pre-disaster cohort and which may be incoming as a result of post-disaster rescue and relief operations.

Meta POP · NET · MOV, 26–30 Aug 2026 Copernicus EMS EMSR927 ReliefWeb/DFS 27 Aug · OCHA #3 28 Aug · PDC 26 Aug · OCHA #4 31 Aug Analyst: situational triage, not verified ground truth

What happened

Trigger → path → downstream effects

On 26 August, an ice-and-rock avalanche is believed to have blocked the Lhende Khola — a Bhote Koshi tributary on the Nepal–China border — forming a debris-dammed lake roughly 20 km upstream of the Miteri Bridge that then burst. The USGS initially logged a M4.4 earthquake at 08:37 local time, then revised it to a M5.2 glacial collapse. The surge travelled roughly 60 km down the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani systems in under a day.

Four reports, one worsening picture

Ground-truth casualty figures by source and cutoff — not a single number

These four reports don't agree, and shouldn't be read as if they do: PDC's figure is a same-day modeled estimate, the other three are successive government-sourced counts as search and rescue proceeded. Read together, the trend is what matters: the confirmed toll rose more than sixfold from the first report to the fourth, and missing-persons figures jumped again between OCHA's third and fourth updates as reporting caught up with the scale of the disaster.

PDC's exposure modeling and the government-sourced counts are not directly comparable methodologies — one estimates who was in harm's way from hazard and baseline population data, the other counts confirmed cases as search and rescue proceeds. Displacement is still only the five tracked sites in Nuwakot, unchanged across three straight OCHA updates — that's a reporting gap, not evidence displacement stopped growing. Update #4 separately reports 10,451 people rescued to date and 20,819 search-and-rescue personnel deployed.

Population variance: crisis vs. baseline

Meta POP · z-score by tile, latest snapshot (31 Aug 04:45 NPT)

Each dot is an ~800 m Meta population tile, colored by how far its most recent reading sits from its own baseline (z-score, capped at ±4). Red = fewer detected people/devices than expected; teal = more, plotted over OpenTopoMap terrain so the corridor's relief is visible under the signal. Dashed outlines mark the approximate rapid-triage zones used throughout this page — bounding boxes, not administrative boundaries. This snapshot is the last of fifteen across five days — see the trajectory section below for the full path here, not just the endpoint.

Baseline Facebook user population magnitude

Meta POP · expected Facebook-app users per tile, pre-crisis

Every "population" figure on this page — here and in the z-score map above — is really a count of Facebook app users Meta's model expects to detect in that tile, not a census population. This pane plots that expected pre-crisis user count directly: each tile's own baseline, so a large anomaly can be weighed against whether it happened in a hamlet or a population center of app users. Values are heavily right-skewed — single digits in the high mountains up to five figures in central Kathmandu (see the range below) — so color is mapped on a log scale, otherwise all but a handful of Kathmandu Valley tiles would look identical.

Five-day population trajectory

Meta POP · % change vs. baseline, all fifteen snapshots

Every district's population-anomaly reading across all five monitoring batches (26–30 Aug), each contributing three snapshots at 12:45, 20:45 and 04:45 NPT — that last one rolling into the next calendar day (dashed dividers mark each batch boundary). Meta's own timestamps are Pacific Time, corrected here to NPT. With five days now in view, the picture is noisier than a two-point comparison suggested: Rasuwa never recovers, it oscillates between roughly –20% and –57% with no clear trend; Dhading sits in a persistent mild deficit (–3% to –13%) rather than a one-way slide; everywhere else stays close to baseline. Rasuwa's brief high point, –20% at 28 Aug 04:45 NPT, lines up with search-and-rescue personnel mobilizing into the district through the 27th — one plausible reading is that SAR teams carrying phones, not returning residents, drove that uptick before it reverted to a deeper deficit.

Network conditions in the impact zone

Meta NET · coverage footprint, 30 Aug 12:45 NPT (latest) vs. 26 Aug 12:45 (first reading, 96h earlier)

Meta's timestamps are Pacific Time; converted to NPT, the first NET snapshot lands ~3.8 hours after the flood's ~09:00 onset — there's no pre-flood reading to compare against. Across the four days since, the story has flipped from what the first 24 hours suggested: Rasuwa's covered-tile count didn't keep falling, it recovered and then grew past its first-reading level, consistent with OCHA's reporting of an active communications-restoration task team and hydropower crews on site. Grey dots are tiles that held coverage at both readings; red rings mark tiles present on 26 Aug that had dropped out by 30 Aug; teal rings mark tiles that newly appeared.

Latest footprint, with 4-day coverage loss/gain marked

Net coverage change, 26→30 Aug

Rasuwa and Nuwakot — the two hardest-hit zones — now show more covered tiles than on 26 Aug, not fewer. That's a genuine infrastructure recovery signal, and it's exactly why the persistently depressed POP signal in Rasuwa (trajectory below) can't be explained away as a connectivity artifact: the towers are back, the detected population isn't.

Movement anomalies

Meta MOV · origin–destination flows, 20:45 & 04:45 NPT, all five batches

Arcs show tile-to-tile movement whose latest (30 Aug) volume deviated most from baseline (z-score, capped at ±4). Rasuwa and Dhading are almost absent from the scored-flow set throughout — too few devices there clear Meta's privacy threshold — so the strongest visible signal sits one tier downstream, on the Kathmandu Valley ↔ Nuwakot corridor: the main access route to the disaster zone. Corridor-wide, high-anomaly flows rose from 1,624 (26 Aug) to a peak of 2,111 (28 Aug), then fell to 848 by 30 Aug — below where they started. Movement disruption spiked mid-week and has since eased past its initial level (table below).

Patterns across the three datasets

Where POP, NET and MOV agree — and where they can't see
The infrastructure story reversed

Rasuwa's network didn't just stop failing — it recovered past its starting point

The first 24 hours looked like confirmed infrastructure collapse: Rasuwa lost 27 of 72 covered tiles (37.5%) between 26 and 27 August. Three more days of NET data changed that story — by 30 August the corridor had recovered most of that loss and added new tiles beyond it, a net +18% versus the first reading. Nuwakot shows the same pattern. This doesn't explain why Rasuwa's population signal stayed suppressed (see below) — it does mean "thin coverage" can no longer be blamed for it.

Not a one-way slide

Dhading's deficit is persistent, not progressive

Dhading tipped negative on Day 2 (+0.1%→–4.6%) and has stayed there since — but it hasn't kept getting worse. Across five days it ranges from –3.0% to –7.6% with no clear trend in either direction: a real, sustained mild deficit, not the emerging crisis a two-point read suggested. NET shows only a small net change there (+0.8%), consistent with a real population effect rather than a connectivity artifact.

Two signals, two stories

Nuwakot's population count barely moved — its traffic swung hard, then settled

Nuwakot's POP reading stays close to flat throughout (mostly +2.0% to +2.3%, with one +6.4% blip) — on population alone, nothing much happened here. Its MOV flow with Kathmandu Valley tells a rockier story: both directions ran positive on Day 1, one leg swung to –22.6% and the other to –30.3% during the mid-week peak, then both settled back to modest positive (+5.8%/+7.6%) by 30 August, close to where they started. A district's headcount can look unremarkable while what's moving through it swings wildly and back — one dataset alone would have missed the whole arc.

The surge faded and stayed faded

Day 1's inbound population spikes settled near baseline and held

Kathmandu Valley (+5.3%→+1.6%), Chitwan (+8.3%→+1.4%), Gorkha (+9.8%→+3.1%) and Tanahu (+6.9%→+0.8%) all show the same shape: a sharp Day 1 inbound anomaly — plausibly displacement, relief staging, hospital transfers — that decayed within a day or two and has stayed low since. Five days in, this reads as a short-lived response surge, not a lasting population shift.

A mid-week spike, not a lasting shift

The Kathmandu↔Nuwakot corridor swung hard, then came back

Day 1 saw two-way surge traffic, both directions above baseline. By Days 2–3 it swung sharply — Nuwakot→Kathmandu fell to –22.6%, then Kathmandu→Nuwakot fell to –30.3% the next day — before both legs recovered to +5.8%/+7.6% by Day 5, close to where they started. Corridor-wide high-anomaly flows trace the same arc: 1,624 → a peak of 2,111 (28 Aug) → 848 (30 Aug), below where they started. The access corridor got rockier mid-week before it calmed down.

Cross-reference with Copernicus

EMSR927's four AOIs still line up with the Meta data — differently than Day 2 suggested

Syaprubesi and Timure sit inside the Rasuwa zone whose cell network has now recovered (rapid mapping still "ongoing," 0–1 products delivered so far) — but whose population signal hasn't followed it up. Bharatpur (Chitwan) sits inside the zone that had the sharpest Day 1 population surge, since faded to near baseline. Both AOIs still mark real ground truth; what they mean has shifted as more data arrived.

Don't read connectivity recovery as human recovery

Rasuwa's network came back. Its detected population didn't. The death toll kept climbing.

Between the first and latest NET readings, Rasuwa's cell coverage recovered and grew past its starting level (+18%). Its population signal did not follow: across the same five days it oscillated between roughly –20% and –65% with no sustained recovery. Meanwhile OCHA's confirmed toll rose from 539 (28 Aug) to 903 (31 Aug). All three can be true at once — restored towers, a population that hasn't come back, and a death toll still being confirmed. No single signal here is the whole story.

Methodology & caveats — read before acting on this
  • Every timestamp on this page has been corrected from Pacific Time to Nepal Time (+12h45m). Meta's raw exports are timestamped PDT, not NPT. Converted correctly, the flood's ~09:00 NPT onset on 26 Aug falls before this dataset's first snapshot (26 Aug 12:45 NPT) — so there is no pre-flood reading anywhere in POP, NET or MOV; every figure on this page describes conditions already ~4 hours or more after onset.
  • Mobile signal ≠ census population. Meta's POP/MOV figures are baseline-normalized counts of detected mobile devices/app users, not verified headcounts. Treat every figure here as a proxy, not a survey result.
  • Z-scores are capped at ±4 by Meta's own methodology. Rasuwa's true anomaly magnitude is understated by every chart on this page.
  • Sparse tiles are suppressed, not zeroed. Differential-privacy thresholds mean very low-population or low-signal tiles simply drop out of the data rather than reporting near-zero — this is the main reason the epicenter itself looks emptier in the data than it should.
  • Every percent-change figure on this page sums only tiles with a paired baseline and crisis reading. Summing baseline unconditionally while treating a missing crisis value as zero would mismatch the denominator against a partial numerator and overstate every deficit — most severely in Rasuwa, where as few as 3–25 of its 73 tiles have a complete reading at any given hour across the fifteen snapshots. Rasuwa's population figures rest on very small, noisy samples throughout; treat them as indicative, not precise. NET's tile-count figures don't depend on this baseline/crisis pairing and are the more reliable Rasuwa signal on this page.
  • NET is five daily snapshots over 96 hours, not continuous monitoring — and all of them are post-event. The first reading is ~3.8 hours after the ~09:00 NPT onset; the last is ~99.8 hours after it. A tower that failed and was restored between two snapshots, or failed after the last one was taken, wouldn't show up as "lost" here — the net-recovery figures shown are a lower bound on how much has actually been restored.
  • Zone boundaries are rectangular bounding boxes drawn for rapid triage, not official administrative or CBS boundaries. Tiles near a boundary may be attributed to the wrong district.
  • The four ground-truth reports don't agree, and that's expected, not an error. PDC's figures are a same-day modeled exposure estimate (26 Aug); ReliefWeb/DFS (27 Aug) and OCHA's Flash Updates #3 (28 Aug) and #4 (31 Aug) are successive government-sourced counts. Every count was explicitly labeled provisional by its own source and rose from one report to the next as search and rescue reached previously cut-off communities — treat the trend as the signal, not any single headline number. Displacement (1,080+, Nuwakot only) is the one figure that hasn't moved across three straight OCHA updates — a reporting gap, not evidence the number is final.
  • This page is a same-day analyst triage for situational awareness. It is not a substitute for the official Copernicus EMSR927 delineation/grading products (activation ongoing) or verified government damage assessments.
